newsitem.title: CHINA: China rubber longs, shorts seen moving to truce.
newsitem.headline: China rubber longs, shorts seen moving to truce.

text.p: Longs and shorts on the China Commodity Futures Exchange have begun negotiations in an effort to call a truce in their battle over the key August 1997 rubber contract, traders said on Tuesday.
But reaching an agreement would not be easy, and both sides could be compelled by the exchange to offset their positions, leading longs to push prices up further, they said.
The August contract on the exchange in southern Hainan province has fluctuated in a wide range in recent weeks as the confrontation between longs and shorts has grown increasingly fierce.
The contract closed last week at 12,445 yuan ($1,501) per tonne, up from 12,120 a week ago. The rises continued, and the contract closed on Tuesday at 12,670 yuan, up 400 yuan from Monday's close.
"Longs and shorts began their negotiations on Monday, but they did not reach any agreement," said a trader in Shanghai.
"With the approach of the delivery month, they are likely to be forced to offset their positions according to exchange regulations," he said.
Under those regulations, every member was permitted to keep 200 lots (1,000 tonnes) from the first day of the delivery month, with excess positions to be offset by the exchange, traders said.
Short positions would be offset at the daily limit-up prices and long positions would be covered at the limit-down prices, they said.
The August contract is due for delivery on August 18. Only two trading days remain ahead of the delivery month.
Longs were sure to push up the price of the August contract in order to limit their own losses even if they were forced to offset their positions at limit-down levels, traders said.
"If longs push the price up to a very high level, they can make profits even though their positions are covered by the exchange at limit-down levels," a Shanghai analyst said.
"In this way, they can also avoid taking physicals," he said.

"It will be a little bit difficult for longs to control the market after we have entered the delivery month, as major longs have to disperse their positions to more members so as not to violate the exchange's regulations," another analyst said.
Open interest in the August contract fell to 199,522 lots from 213,608 lots a week ago as retail investors retreated, traders said.
But they added that major longs had not reduced their open interest.
The exchange's rubber stocks had surged to 121,696 tonnes by the end of last week, compared with 84,536 tonnes a week ago, traders said.
